script.title: Why Laika Really Went to Space

lines: A technician kissed a little dog's nose, then closed the hatch on her.
In October 1957, Sputnik 1 was a triumph.
Nikita Khrushchev wanted a space spectacular by the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution.
That left less than four weeks.
Sergei Korolev proposed that a dog be placed in the satellite.
Soviet engineers had long planned a dog in orbit before any human.
Since 1951, they had lofted 12 dogs on short flights.
They chose Laika, a stray from the streets of Moscow.
Scientists assumed strays had already learned to endure cold and hunger.
She was kept in smaller and smaller cages for up to twenty days.
You see, it's like dipping a toe in the water before you jump in.
Nobody knew if a living body could survive being launched into orbit.
Wires on her body sent her breathing, pulse and blood pressure to the ground.
Her heart rate jumped from 103 to 240 beats a minute.
But the technology to come back through the atmosphere did not exist yet.
Laika died hours into the flight, on the fourth orbit.
In 1998, Oleg Gazenko, who trained her, said they did not learn enough to justify her death.

claims.claim: One of the technicians said: after placing Laika in the container and before closing the hatch, we kissed her nose and wished her bon voyage, knowing that she would not survive the flight.

After the success of Sputnik 1 in October 1957, Khrushchev wanted a spacecraft launched to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the October Revolution, a 'space spectacular'; the decision left less than four weeks to design and build the spacecraft.

Sergei Korolev proposed that a dog be placed in the satellite; Soviet rocket engineers had long intended a canine orbit before attempting human spaceflight; since 1951 they had lofted 12 dogs into sub-orbital space.

Laika was a stray from the streets of Moscow; Soviet scientists assumed strays had already learned to endure extreme cold and hunger; the dogs were kept in progressively smaller cages for periods of up to twenty days.

The experiment aimed to prove that a living organism could survive being launched into orbit; sensors measured breathing, pulse and blood pressure; her heart rate was 103 beats/min before launch and 240 beats/min during early acceleration.
As the technology to re-enter the atmosphere had not yet been developed, Laika's survival was never expected; the cabin overheated and she died hours into the flight, on the craft's fourth orbit.
In 1998 Oleg Gazenko, one of the scientists who trained Laika, said: We did not learn enough from this mission to justify the death of the dog.

cast.technician: a 28 year old Soviet technician, stocky build, a round pale face, short cropped brown hair, a small scar on his chin, a white lab coat over a grey wool sweater, 1950s
cast.khrushchev: a 63 year old stout Soviet leader, a completely bald round head, heavy jowls, a wide gap-toothed grin, small blue eyes, a dark grey suit with two gold star medals on the chest, 1950s
cast.korolev: a 50 year old broad-shouldered Soviet rocket designer, a heavy square face, thick dark eyebrows, dark wavy hair combed back, a brown leather jacket over a white open-collared shirt, 1950s
cast.yazdovsky: a 44 year old lean Soviet doctor, a long narrow face, a neat black moustache, thick black hair parted on the side, round wire spectacles, a white lab coat over a dark blue tie, 1950s
cast.gazenko: an 80 year old thin Russian scientist, a long lined face, white hair combed straight back, large square glasses, a navy blue cardigan over a pale blue shirt, 1990s
